fetched_contents.text: Dysmenorrhea, Endometriosis and Chronic Pelvic Pain in Adolescents Abstract Most adolescents will experience discomfort during menstruation. Due to normalization of dysmenorrhea, there is delay to diagnosis and treatment. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatories are a first line treatment. Adolescents can safely be offered menstrual suppression with combined hormonal contraception, and progestin-only options. When the above are ineffective, gonadotropin releasing hormone agonists with add back treatment can be considered. Transabdominal ultrasound is indicated when first line treatments do not improve symptoms. Endometriosis should be considered in adolescents who experience ongoing pain despite medical treatment. If laparoscopy is performed and endometriosis visualized, it should be treated with either excision or ablation. Women with endometriosis should be counselled on menstrual suppression until fertility is desired. Management of chronic pain requires the involvement of a multi-disciplinary team. Keywords: Dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, endometriosis Introduction The majority (70-93%) of adolescents have discomfort associated with menstruation (1,2). Dysmenorrhea is the most common reason for missed school and activities (3). Up to 20-40% report missed school due to dysmenorrhea, and 40% report a negative effect on school performance and concentration (4). Adolescents with severe dysmenorrhea have impaired quality of life and are at increased risk for depression and anxiety (5). They present later for assessment, see multiple physicians, and suffer more, compared to adults (4). Functional impairment is the primary reason for seeking medical care in adolescents with dysmenorrhea (6). Health care practitioners (HCP) should not normalize dysmenorrhea. Adolescent women should be offered treatment and further investigation for ongoing pain (7). Primary dysmenorrhea is menstrual pain in the absence of pelvic pathology. Secondary dysmenorrhea is menstrual pain in the presence of pelvic pathology or due to a recognized medical condition. Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnosis for pelvic pain is seen in Table 1. Table 1. Differential diagnosis for pelvic pain. History Information about age of menarche, cycle regularity, duration of menses, amount of bleeding, and time elapsed between onset of menarche and dysmenorrhea should be elicited. Pain history should encompass onset, duration, severity, aggravating and alleviating factors, and relationship to menses. Urinary, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal and psychological symptoms should be documented. The degree of functional impairment, including absence/avoidance of school, social and sports activities should be explored (13). Adolescents should be interviewed with caregivers and independently; parental modeling may influence pain reporting and perception (14). Sexual history, if appropriate, should include presence of dyspareunia, history of sexually transmitted or pelvic infections, and sexual violence. Previous treatment, including medications, dosage and timing should be documented. One study reported that although 70% of adolescents took over-the-counter medications, only 31% followed recommended dosing, and only 16% took analgesics prophylactically (2). Physical Examination Height, weight, and vital signs should be recorded. Further examination can be delayed until a later visit. Prior to initiating hormonal treatment, only blood pressure must be documented (15). HCP should explain the steps and elicit frequent feedback. Abdomen: Light and deep palpation is performed for masses and tenderness. A cotton swab can be used to assess for allodynia (16). Myofascial pain is assessed by asking the patient to contract their abdominal wall muscles while palpating an area of tenderness (Carnett’s test). Increased pain indicates a myofascial trigger point as the intraperitoneal organs are protected (10). Pelvis: The adolescent should be offered a mirror to assist with the educational gynecologic exam. Begin with examination of the external genitalia. Gentle traction of the labia can allow visualization of the introitus. A cotton swab can be used to gently apply pressure to the vaginal introitus to map out points of increased pain, indicating provoked vestibulodynia (17). Internal pelvic examination should be limited to sexually active patients, and may not be feasible due to anxiety, patient expectations, or pain (10). In adolescents that can tolerate a single digit vaginal exam, the bladder neck, levator ani, cervix, adnexa and uterosacral ligaments should be palpated for tenderness. Uterosacral nodules indicative of deep invasive endometriosis are rare adolescents (6,18). If there is concern about obstruction, a moistened cotton swab can be gently inserted into the vagina (19). Digital rectal examination may also be helpful to appreciate hematocolpos; a bulge may be palpated in the vagina. Primary Dysmenorrhea Primary Dysmenorrhea is associated with anovulatory cycles and usually presents 6-12 months post-menarche (8). Pain is due to increased uterine contractility and elevated prostaglandin levels as the ischemic endometrial lining is sloughed off (1,9,20). Prevalence: Dysmenorrhea is estimated to affect 70-93% of young women (1,2). Pathogenesis: Menstrual pain results from vasoconstriction and inflammation. Prostaglandins, leukotrienes and vasopressin are key drivers (21). Omega-6 Fatty acids, including arachidonic acid, are released with progesterone withdrawal, increasing local prostaglandin and leukotriene production (3,21,22). Prostaglandins induce myometrial contractility, vasoconstriction and uterine ischemia (3,21,22). Additional prostaglandin effects include headaches, nausea, bloating, vomiting and diarrhea (21). fetched_contents.text: Evaluation and Treatment of Chronic Pelvic Pain ---------------------------------------- Chronic pelvic pain is a multifactorial condition best managed through interdisciplinary care that integrates behavioral, pharmacologic, and surgical treatments using shared decision making. Abstract Chronic pelvic pain (CPP) is a complex and often debilitating condition that affects 15–26% of women worldwide. It is defined as pain perceived to originate from pelvic organs or structures that typically lasts longer than 6 months and is often associated with negative cognitive, behavioral, sexual, and emotional consequences. Chronic pelvic pain is not a single disease but rather a symptom with many potential causes, with most patients having multiple contributing conditions. This article provides an overview of the evaluation and management of CPP for obstetrician–gynecologists. We recommend an organ system–based approach to diagnosis, recognizing that any combination of gynecologic, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, urologic, neurologic, and vascular sources is a possible cause. Effective management integrates behavioral, pharmacologic, and surgical strategies tailored to the suspected pain mechanisms in each patient. Educating patients about pain physiology, including the interaction between peripheral pathology and central pain amplification, is essential. Although CPP is not always curable, patients can experience significant and meaningful improvement in pain, function, and quality of life through long-term interdisciplinary support. Establishing a strong therapeutic relationship, validating patients' experiences, and empowering patients to take an active role in their care are central to effective management. Shared decision making, collaborative goal setting, and establishing clear expectations support sustained engagement and functional improvement. ---------------------------------------- Chronic pelvic pain (CPP) is an often debilitating condition that affects 15–26% of women worldwide.1 Although there is no consensus among professional societies on the definition of CPP or minimal duration of pain required for diagnosis, the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists defines it as, “pain symptoms perceived to originate from pelvic organs/structures typically lasting more than 6 months” that “is often associated with negative cognitive, behavioral, sexual and emotional consequences as well as with symptoms of lower urinary tract, sexual, bowel, pelvic floor, myofascial, or gynecologic dysfunction.”2 There is wide variation in the frequency, pattern, and location of pain in patients with CPP. Pain may be intermittent or constant, exhibit a cyclical pattern that is temporally associated with the menstrual cycle (eg, ovulatory pain or dysmenorrhea), or can occur when not menstruating (nonmenstrual pelvic pain). Pain can also be localized to a single site or involve multiple pelvic regions. Furthermore, there is no consensus among professional societies regarding the minimum duration of pain required for diagnosis, with some defining CPP as pain lasting 3 months or longer and others using a threshold of 6 months or longer.3 The substantial symptom burden frequently leads to repeated surgical procedures and prolonged use of medical therapies. On average, individuals with CPP have a higher number of office visits, emergency department visits, hospitalizations, diagnostic testing, medication use (including opioids), and surgical procedures compared with those without CPP.4,5 Despite these interventions, many experience persistent pain and distress and report feeling stigmatized and dismissed,6,7 which contribute to impaired emotional health, reduced work productivity, and lower quality of life.8,9 PATHOPHYSIOLOGY Chronic pelvic pain is not a single disease but rather a symptom with many potential causes, often with multiple contributing conditions in affected individuals. These include disorders with identifiable gynecologic pathology (eg, endometriosis) and others better characterized as functional pain syndromes (eg, irritable bowel syndrome). Many conditions associated with CPP are part of the broader chronic overlapping pain conditions recognized by the National Institutes of Health, which include fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, chronic migraine, chronic tension-type headache, temporomandibular joint disorder, chronic low back pain, irritable bowel syndrome, interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome, vulvodynia, and endometriosis.10 Chronic overlapping pain conditions affect predominantly women and frequently co-occur in the same individual. For example, one insurance claims–based study reported that individuals with endometriosis have significantly elevated odds of co-occurring chronic pain conditions, including a 15.6-fold increase for vulvodynia, 18.6-fold for irritable bowel syndrome, 10-fold for fibromyalgia, fivefold for interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome, and 3.2-fold for migraine headaches.11 Chronic overlapping pain conditions share common risk factors and pathophysiologic mechanisms, most notably central nervous system sensitization that promotes chronic pain at multiple levels (ie, spinal, subcortical, cortical). The terms nociplastic pain, centralized pain, and central sensitization are overlapping concepts that have been used to describe this phenomenon.11–13 Nociplastic pain mechanisms are thought to be a common feature of chronic overlapping pain conditions, including CPP. Physical examination for adolescents suspected of endometriosis should be focused, patient-centered, and guided by the clinical context rather than a routine full genital exam. The evidence supports a careful pelvic exam that includes external genitalia, a speculum and bimanual exam, and, under some circumstances, a rectovaginal exam [N3-F3]. For adolescents, this is particularly important because the exam should be performed in a way that respects developmental and psychosocial context, and because internal pelvic examination may be limited or delayed if the adolescent is anxious, has pain, or is not sexually active [N1-F1].

### Components of a focused pelvic exam appropriate for adolescents
A focused adolescent pelvic exam should begin with inspection of the external genitalia and then proceed to a speculum and bimanual exam [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that rectovaginal examination may be appropriate when better characterization of the posterior pelvis is needed [N3-F3]. In adolescents, the exam should be adapted to the patient’s readiness, anxiety level, and ability to tolerate internal examination. The same source emphasizes that external genitalia and internal genitalia are both part of the pelvic exam [N3-F3]. The UpToDate evidence similarly states that physical examination should include a pelvic examination that checks for tenderness or nodules of the cul-de-sac or uterosacral ligaments [N6-R2]. That is a helpful shorthand for what should be palpated during a focused exam.

### Findings that are suggestive of endometriosis versus nonspecific findings
The most suggestive endometriosis findings on exam are tender nodules along thickened uterosacral ligaments, posterior uterus, or other sites where deep infiltrating endometriosis can be felt [N3-R5]. The evidence also notes that uterosacral ligament nodularity and firm nodules on rectovaginal or bimanual exam strongly suggest deep infiltrating endometriosis [N3-R2]. By contrast, nonspecific findings include tenderness in the pelvis, pain provoked by pressure, or findings that can be explained by other pelvic conditions rather than endometriosis [N3-R5]. The pelvic exam should therefore be interpreted alongside the history and other diagnostic clues rather than as a standalone test.

### When and how to perform rectovaginal or other specialized exams
Rectovaginal examination is indicated when the clinician needs better characterization of the posterior pelvis [N3-F3]. The evidence also supports this approach because it can help identify uterosacral nodules and other deep infiltrating findings [N3-R2]. However, in adolescents, this exam should be performed carefully and only when clinically indicated. The evidence notes that internal pelvic examination should be limited to sexually active patients, and may not be feasible due to anxiety, patient expectations, or pain [N1-F1]. Thus, rectovaginal or specialized exams should be reserved for cases where the history and initial exam raise suspicion of deep endometriosis, and performed with clear communication and patient consent [N3-F3].

### How to document findings in a way that supports diagnosis
Documentation should be thorough and structured. The evidence emphasizes that findings should be recorded in a way that supports diagnosis, including details of tenderness, nodule characteristics, and the location of pain [N3-R5]. It also notes that physical findings are part of the broader diagnostic workup, not just a routine exam [N3-F3]. A helpful approach is to record whether uterosacral ligaments are thickened or tender, whether posterior uterine tenderness is present, and whether rectovaginal examination reveals firm nodules or other suspicious findings [N3-R2][N3-R5]. These notes help distinguish endometriosis from nonspecific pelvic pain and support subsequent imaging or specialist referral [N3-F3].
node_outputs.N10:
Differentiating endometriosis from other causes of pelvic pain in adolescents requires combining history, physical findings, and red flags with a broad differential diagnosis. The evidence shows that adolescents with endometriosis often present with dysmenorrhea, chronic pelvic pain, and pain that worsens with bowel movement, urination, or sexual activity [N2-R2][N2-R5]. At the same time, many pelvic pain conditions in adolescents overlap with functional or musculoskeletal causes, making endometriosis harder to diagnose without careful evaluation [N2-F2].

### Red flags that point toward endometriosis rather than a different diagnosis
The strongest red flags for endometriosis in adolescents include:
- Dysmenorrhea that is severe or worsening despite treatment [N1-F1][N2-R2]
- Pelvic pain that worsens with bowel movement, urination, or sexual activity [N2-R5]
- Tenderness or nodules on pelvic exam, especially along uterosacral ligaments or posterior uterus [N3-R2][N3-R5]
- A history of delayed diagnosis and normalization of dysmenorrhea [N1-F1]
- Family history of endometriosis or related conditions [N6-R3][N6-R4]

These red flags help distinguish endometriosis from other pelvic pain conditions by linking symptoms to anatomical or hormonal mechanisms rather than purely functional or musculoskeletal causes [N2-F2]. The evidence also emphasizes that adolescents with endometriosis may present with nonmenstrual pelvic pain, which should not be dismissed as “just growing pains” [N2-F2].

### Non-endometriosis causes that must be considered
The differential diagnosis is broad. The evidence includes several important non-endometriosis causes:
- Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)
- Ovarian torsion
- Ruptured ovarian cyst
- Appendicitis
- Ovarian cysts and other gynecological/obstetrical causes [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]
- Functional pain conditions, including irritable bowel syndrome, vulvodynia, fibromyalgia, chronic migraine, and interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome [N2-F2]
- Myofascial pain and other musculoskeletal causes [N2-F2]

These conditions must be considered because they can mimic endometriosis, especially when adolescents present with chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, or pain related to activity or intercourse [N2-F2][N2-R4]. The evidence also highlights that CPP can have multiple contributing conditions, including gynecologic pathology and functional pain syndromes [N2-F2].

### When imaging is indicated and what it can show
Imaging is indicated when the history and physical exam are inconclusive, or when endometriosis is suspected despite a negative physical exam. The evidence supports ultrasound and MRI as the main imaging modalities [N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-R5]. A transabdominal ultrasound is helpful for identifying ovarian endometriomas but has a limited role in evaluating deep endometriosis [N4-R1]. MRI is particularly useful for rectosigmoid endometriosis and for treatment planning [N4-R4]. The UpToDate guidance also notes that MRI and transvaginal ultrasonography are recommended in the evaluation of suspected endometriosis [N6-R5]. In adolescents, MRI is often preferred when transvaginal ultrasound is not feasible or informative [N4-R5].

### When referral to a specialist is appropriate
Referral to a specialist should be considered when the diagnosis remains uncertain, when symptoms are refractory to first-line treatment, or when imaging suggests deep or complex endometriosis. The evidence supports specialist involvement because adolescents may need a multidisciplinary approach, especially if there is ongoing pain despite medical treatment [N1-F1][N6-R3]. Laparoscopic findings may also guide management [N4-R5]. The evidence further notes that adolescents with endometriosis may require counseling on menstrual suppression and may benefit from a multi-disciplinary team for chronic pain management [N1-F1]. Therefore, referral to a gynecologist or endometriosis specialist is appropriate when history, physical findings, and imaging do not confirm a clear alternative diagnosis, or when the adolescent’s pain is not adequately controlled with initial treatment [N4-R2][N6-R3].
node_outputs.N8:
The initial patient history for adolescents suspected of endometriosis should be comprehensive but developmentally sensitive. The evidence supports a history that includes menstrual history, dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain characteristics, sexual and reproductive history, family history, and psychosocial context [N1-F1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. This approach is especially important in adolescents, because pain normalization and delayed diagnosis are common [N1-F1].

### Symptoms and symptom patterns that are most informative
The most informative symptoms are dysmenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, and acyclic pelvic pain [N1-R5]. The evidence also notes that nonmenstrual pelvic pain can occur, and that pain may be aggravated by activity, intercourse, bowel movements, or urination [N2-R2][N2-R5]. Pain patterns that are particularly concerning for endometriosis include severe dysmenorrhea that does not improve with standard treatment, pain that worsens with bowel movement or urination, and pain that is provoked during gynecologic examination [N1-F1][N2-R5]. The evidence also emphasizes that adolescents may report other associated symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headaches, tiredness, back pain, and irritable mood [N2-R3].

### Menstrual history, including age of menarche and cycle regularity
Menstrual history is central to the evaluation. The evidence notes that age of menarche, cycle regularity, duration of menses, and the time elapsed between onset of menarche and dysmenorrhea should be elicited [N1-F1]. This is important because primary dysmenorrhea is often associated with anovulatory cycles and usually presents 6–12 months post-menarche [N1-F1]. Secondary dysmenorrhea, by contrast, is associated with pelvic pathology and may be more severe or persistent [N1-F1]. The evidence also highlights that adolescents should be asked about the degree of functional impairment, including absence or avoidance of school, social, and sports activities [N1-F1].

### Pelvic pain characteristics and how they relate to activity or intercourse
Pelvic pain should be described in terms of onset, duration, severity, aggravating and alleviating factors, and relationship to menses [N1-F1]. The evidence specifically notes that pain may be cyclic, acyclic, or accompanied by bowel or urinary symptoms [N1-F1]. It also states that endometriosis pain can worsen with bowel movement or urination and can be associated with painful tampon insertion or dyspareunia [N2-R5]. These details are important because they help distinguish endometriosis from other pelvic pain conditions, especially functional pain syndromes [N2-F2].

### Sexual and reproductive history relevant to diagnosis
Sexual and reproductive history is relevant because endometriosis may present with dyspareunia, and adolescents may also have a history of sexually transmitted infections or sexual violence [N1-F1]. The evidence notes that the first assessment should include a sexual history, including presence of dyspareunia, history of sexually transmitted or pelvic infections, and sexual violence [N1-F1]. It also notes that previous treatment, including medications, dosage, and timing, should be documented [N1-F1]. This history is important for assessing the full burden of pain and identifying conditions that may overlap with endometriosis [N2-F2].

### Family history of endometriosis or related conditions
Family history is an important red flag. The evidence notes that endometriosis should be considered in adolescents who experience ongoing pain despite medical treatment [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that the first assessment should include a family history of endometriosis or related conditions [N6-R3]. Family history is especially useful because endometriosis is genetically influenced and may run in families [N6-R3]. Including family history helps identify patients at higher risk and supports early investigation [N6-R3].

### Psychosocial and developmental context that may affect symptom reporting
The psychosocial and developmental context is central to history-taking in adolescents. The evidence states that adolescents should be interviewed with caregivers and independently, because parental modeling may influence pain reporting and perception [N1-F1]. It also notes that health care practitioners should not normalize dysmenorrhea, because normalization can delay diagnosis and treatment [N1-F1]. Adolescents may also experience anxiety, depression, and impaired quality of life, which can affect symptom reporting and functional impairment [N1-F1][N7-R4]. The evidence further notes that the impact of dysmenorrhea on quality of life is exacerbated by severity of pain and delay of diagnosis [N7-R5]. Therefore, the history should include questions about school attendance, social and sports activities, and emotional well-being [N1-F1].

Adolescents with endometriosis present differently from adults, and this has important diagnostic implications. The evidence shows that adolescents often experience dysmenorrhea and pelvic pain that is normalized or delayed in diagnosis because it is common for them to endure pain without seeking timely evaluation [N1-F1]. Adolescents can also present with symptoms that overlap with functional pain syndromes, making endometriosis harder to distinguish from other pelvic pain conditions [N2-F2].

### How adolescents with endometriosis differ from adult patients
Adolescents differ from adults in several ways. First, they often present with dysmenorrhea that is severe or persistent despite treatment, and this can be the first sign of endometriosis [N1-F1][N2-R2]. Second, adolescents may experience pain that worsens with bowel movement, urination, or sexual activity, which can be a red flag for deep endometriosis [N2-R5]. Third, adolescents may have a family history of endometriosis or related conditions, which increases suspicion [N6-R3]. Fourth, adolescents may be more likely to normalize pain, which delays diagnosis and treatment [N1-F1]. ## Essential components of the initial clinical evaluation and patient history for adolescents suspected of having endometriosis

Assessing adolescents suspected of having endometriosis requires a structured, developmentally sensitive approach that combines a thorough patient history, focused physical examination, and awareness of the broader differential diagnosis. The evidence in the branch reports points to a clear pattern: adolescents often present with dysmenorrhea and pelvic pain that may be normalized or delayed in diagnosis, so clinicians must avoid routine dismissal and carefully evaluate symptoms, menstrual history, and psychosocial context [N1-F1][N2-F2][N7-R4].

### 1. Initial patient history: what should be included

The initial history should be comprehensive but developmentally appropriate. It should include:

- **Symptoms and symptom patterns that are most informative**  
  The most informative symptoms are dysmenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, and acyclic pelvic pain [N1-R5]. The evidence also notes that pain may be aggravated by activity, intercourse, bowel movements, or urination, and may be accompanied by nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headaches, tiredness, back pain, or irritability [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. Pain patterns that are especially concerning for endometriosis include severe dysmenorrhea that does not improve with standard treatment, pain that worsens with bowel movement or urination, and pain that is provoked during gynecologic examination [N1-F1][N2-R5]. The branch report also emphasizes that adolescents may report other associated symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headaches, tiredness, back pain, and irritable mood [N2-R3].

- **Menstrual history, including age of menarche and cycle regularity**  
  Menstrual history is central. The evidence notes that age of menarche, cycle regularity, duration of menses, and the time elapsed between onset of menarche and dysmenorrhea should be elicited [N1-F1]. This is important because primary dysmenorrhea is often associated with anovulatory cycles and usually presents 6–12 months post-menarche [N1-F1]. Secondary dysmenorrhea, by contrast, is associated with pelvic pathology and may be more severe or persistent [N1-F1]. The branch report also highlights that the history should include questions about the degree of functional impairment, including absence or avoidance of school, social, and sports activities [N1-F1].

- **Pelvic pain characteristics and how they relate to activity or intercourse**  
  Pelvic pain should be described in terms of onset, duration, severity, aggravating and alleviating factors, and relationship to menses [N1-F1]. The evidence specifically notes that pain may be cyclic, acyclic, or accompanied by bowel or urinary symptoms [N1-F1]. It also states that endometriosis pain can worsen with bowel movement or urination and can be associated with painful tampon insertion or dyspareunia [N2-R5]. These details are important because they help distinguish endometriosis from other pelvic pain conditions, especially functional pain syndromes [N2-F2].

- **Sexual and reproductive history relevant to diagnosis**  
  Sexual and reproductive history is relevant because endometriosis may present with dyspareunia, and adolescents may also have a history of sexually transmitted infections or sexual violence [N1-F1]. The evidence notes that the first assessment should include a sexual history, including presence of dyspareunia, history of sexually transmitted or pelvic infections, and sexual violence [N1-F1]. It also notes that previous treatment, including medications, dosage, and timing, should be documented [N1-F1]. This history is important for assessing the full burden of pain and identifying conditions that may overlap with endometriosis [N2-F2].

- **Family history of endometriosis or related conditions**  
  Family history is an important red flag. The evidence notes that endometriosis should be considered in adolescents who experience ongoing pain despite medical treatment [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that the first assessment should include a family history of endometriosis or related conditions [N6-R3]. Family history is especially useful because endometriosis is genetically influenced and may run in families [N6-R3]. Including family history helps identify patients at higher risk and supports early investigation [N6-R3].

- **Psychosocial and developmental context that may affect symptom reporting**  
  The psychosocial and developmental context is central to history-taking in adolescents. The evidence states that adolescents should be interviewed with caregivers and independently, because parental modeling may influence pain reporting and perception [N1-F1]. It also notes that health care practitioners should not normalize dysmenorrhea, because normalization can delay diagnosis and treatment [N1-F1]. Adolescents may also experience anxiety, depression, and impaired quality of life, which can affect symptom reporting and functional impairment [N1-F1][N7-R4]. The evidence further notes that the impact of dysmenorrhea on quality of life is exacerbated by severity of pain and delay of diagnosis [N7-R5]. Therefore, the history should include questions about school attendance, social and sports activities, and emotional well-being [N1-F1].

### 2. Physical examination: what should be included

The physical examination should be focused, patient-centered, and guided by the clinical context rather than a routine full genital exam [N3-F3]. For adolescents, this is especially important because the exam should be adapted to the patient’s readiness, anxiety level, and ability to tolerate internal examination [N1-F1]. The evidence supports a careful pelvic exam that includes external genitalia, a speculum and bimanual exam, and, under some circumstances, a rectovaginal exam [N3-F3]. The branch report also notes that physical findings are part of the broader diagnostic workup, not just a routine exam [N3-F3].

#### Components of a focused pelvic exam appropriate for adolescents
A focused adolescent pelvic exam should begin with inspection of the external genitalia and then proceed to a speculum and bimanual exam [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that rectovaginal examination may be appropriate when better characterization of the posterior pelvis is needed [N3-F3]. In adolescents, the exam should be performed with clear communication and patient consent, and internal pelvic examination should be limited to sexually active patients when feasible [N1-F1].

#### Findings that are suggestive of endometriosis versus nonspecific findings
The most suggestive endometriosis findings on exam are tender nodules along thickened uterosacral ligaments, posterior uterus, or other sites where deep infiltrating endometriosis can be felt [N3-R5]. The evidence also notes that uterosacral ligament nodularity and firm nodules on rectovaginal or bimanual exam strongly suggest deep infiltrating endometriosis [N3-R2]. By contrast, nonspecific findings include tenderness in the pelvis, pain provoked by pressure, or findings that can be explained by other pelvic conditions rather than endometriosis [N3-R5]. The pelvic exam should therefore be interpreted alongside the history and other diagnostic clues rather than as a standalone test [N3-R5].

#### When and how to perform rectovaginal or other specialized exams
Rectovaginal examination is indicated when the clinician needs better characterization of the posterior pelvis [N3-F3]. The evidence supports this approach because it can help identify uterosacral nodules and other deep infiltrating findings [N3-R2]. However, in adolescents, this exam should be performed carefully and only when clinically indicated. The evidence notes that internal pelvic examination should be limited to sexually active patients, and may not be feasible due to anxiety, patient expectations, or pain [N1-F1]. Thus, rectovaginal or specialized exams should be reserved for cases where the history and initial exam raise suspicion of deep endometriosis, and performed with clear communication and patient consent [N3-F3].

#### How to document findings in a way that supports diagnosis
Documentation should be thorough and structured. The evidence emphasizes that findings should be recorded in a way that supports diagnosis, including details of tenderness, nodule characteristics, and the location of pain [N3-R5]. It also notes that physical findings are part of the broader diagnostic workup, not just a routine exam [N3-F3]. A helpful approach is to record whether uterosacral ligaments are thickened or tender, whether posterior uterine tenderness is present, and whether rectovaginal examination reveals firm nodules or other suspicious findings [N3-R2][N3-R5]. These notes help distinguish endometriosis from nonspecific pelvic pain and support subsequent imaging or specialist referral [N3-F3].

### 3. Differentiating endometriosis from other causes of pelvic pain

Differentiating endometriosis from other causes of pelvic pain in adolescents requires combining history, physical findings, and red flags with a broad differential diagnosis [N2-F2]. The evidence shows that adolescents with endometriosis often present with dysmenorrhea, chronic pelvic pain, and pain that worsens with bowel movement, urination, or sexual activity [N2-R2][N2-R5]. At the same time, many pelvic pain conditions in adolescents overlap with functional or musculoskeletal causes, making endometriosis harder to diagnose without careful evaluation [N2-F2].

#### Red flags that point toward endometriosis rather than a different diagnosis
The strongest red flags for endometriosis in adolescents include:
- Dysmenorrhea that is severe or worsening despite treatment [N1-F1][N2-R2]
- Pelvic pain that worsens with bowel movement, urination, or sexual activity [N2-R5]
- Tenderness or nodules on pelvic exam, especially along uterosacral ligaments or posterior uterus [N3-R2][N3-R5]
- A history of delayed diagnosis and normalization of dysmenorrhea [N1-F1]
- Family history of endometriosis or related conditions [N6-R3][N6-R4]

These red flags help distinguish endometriosis from other pelvic pain conditions by linking symptoms to anatomical or hormonal mechanisms rather than purely functional or musculoskeletal causes [N2-F2].

#### Non-endometriosis causes that must be considered
The differential diagnosis is broad. The evidence includes several important non-endometriosis causes:
- Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)
- Ovarian torsion
- Ruptured ovarian cyst
- Appendicitis
- Ovarian cysts and other gynecological/obstetrical causes [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]
- Functional pain conditions, including irritable bowel syndrome, vulvodynia, fibromyalgia, chronic migraine, and interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome [N2-F2]
- Myofascial pain and other musculoskeletal causes [N2-F2]

These conditions must be considered because they can mimic endometriosis, especially when adolescents present with chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, or pain related to activity or intercourse [N2-F2][N2-R4]. The evidence also highlights that chronic pelvic pain can have multiple contributing conditions, including gynecologic pathology and functional pain syndromes [N2-F2].

#### When imaging is indicated and what it can show
Imaging is indicated when the history and physical exam are inconclusive, or when endometriosis is suspected despite a negative physical exam. The evidence supports ultrasound and MRI as the main imaging modalities [N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-R5]. A transabdominal ultrasound is helpful for identifying ovarian endometriomas but has a limited role in evaluating deep endometriosis [N4-R1]. MRI is particularly useful for rectosigmoid endometriosis and for treatment planning [N4-R4]. The UpToDate guidance also notes that MRI and transvaginal ultrasonography are recommended in the evaluation of suspected endometriosis [N6-R5]. In adolescents, MRI is often preferred when transvaginal ultrasound is not feasible or informative [N4-R5].

#### When referral to a specialist is appropriate
Referral to a specialist should be considered when the diagnosis remains uncertain, when symptoms are refractory to first-line treatment, or when imaging suggests deep or complex endometriosis. The evidence supports specialist involvement because adolescents may need a multidisciplinary approach, especially if there is ongoing pain despite medical treatment [N1-F1][N6-R3]. Laparoscopic findings may also guide management [N4-R5]. The evidence further notes that adolescents with endometriosis may require counseling on menstrual suppression and may benefit from a multidisciplinary team for chronic pain management [N1-F1]. Therefore, referral to a gynecologist or endometriosis specialist is appropriate when history, physical findings, and imaging do not confirm a clear alternative diagnosis, or when the adolescent’s pain is not adequately controlled with initial treatment [N4-R2][N6-R3].

### 4. Adolescents’ presentation and diagnostic challenges

Adolescents with endometriosis present differently from adults, and this has important diagnostic implications. The evidence shows that adolescents often experience dysmenorrhea and pelvic pain that is normalized or delayed in diagnosis because it is common for them to endure pain without seeking timely evaluation [N1-F1]. Adolescents can also present with symptoms that overlap with functional pain syndromes, making endometriosis harder to distinguish from other pelvic pain conditions [N2-F2].

#### How adolescents with endometriosis differ from adult patients
Adolescents differ from adults in several ways. First, they often present with dysmenorrhea that is severe or persistent despite treatment, and this can be the first sign of endometriosis [N1-F1][N2-R2]. Second, adolescents may experience pain that worsens with bowel movement, urination, or sexual activity, which can be a red flag for deep endometriosis [N2-R5]. Third, adolescents may have a family history of endometriosis or related conditions, which increases suspicion [N6-R3]. ### 5. Bottom line: what should clinicians prioritize

Clinicians evaluating adolescents suspected of having endometriosis should prioritize:
1. A thorough, developmentally sensitive history covering dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, menstrual history, sexual and reproductive history, family history, and psychosocial context [N1-F1][N6-R3][N6-R4][N7-R4].
2. A focused, patient-centered physical examination including external genitalia, speculum and bimanual exam, and rectovaginal exam when clinically indicated [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R5].
3. Awareness of red flags such as severe dysmenorrhea, pain worsening with bowel movement/urination/intercourse, uterosacral or posterior uterine tenderness, and family history [N2-R2][N2-R5][N3-R2][N3-R5][N6-R3].
4. Broad differential diagnosis including PID, ovarian torsion, ruptured ovarian cyst, appendicitis, functional pain syndromes, and musculoskeletal causes [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5][N2-F2].
5. Imaging with ultrasound and MRI when the history and physical exam are inconclusive or when deep endometriosis is suspected [N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R5].
6. Referral to a specialist when the diagnosis remains uncertain, symptoms are refractory, or imaging suggests complex disease [N4-R2][N6-R3].

Physical examination for adolescents suspected of endometriosis should be focused, patient-centered, and guided by the clinical context rather than a routine full genital exam. The evidence supports a careful pelvic exam that includes external genitalia, a speculum and bimanual exam, and, under some circumstances, a rectovaginal exam [N3-F3]. For adolescents, this is particularly important because the exam should be performed in a way that respects developmental and psychosocial context, and because internal pelvic examination may be limited or delayed if the adolescent is anxious, has pain, or is not sexually active [N1-F1].

### Components of a focused pelvic exam appropriate for adolescents
A focused adolescent pelvic exam should begin with inspection of the external genitalia and then proceed to a speculum and bimanual exam [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that rectovaginal examination may be appropriate when better characterization of the posterior pelvis is needed [N3-F3]. In adolescents, the exam should be adapted to the patient’s readiness, anxiety level, and ability to tolerate internal examination. The same source emphasizes that external genitalia and internal genitalia are both part of the pelvic exam [N3-F3]. The UpToDate evidence similarly states that physical examination should include a pelvic examination that checks for tenderness or nodules of the cul-de-sac or uterosacral ligaments [N6-R2]. That is a helpful shorthand for what should be palpated during a focused exam.

### Findings that are suggestive of endometriosis versus nonspecific findings
The most suggestive endometriosis findings on exam are tender nodules along thickened uterosacral ligaments, posterior uterus, or other sites where deep infiltrating endometriosis can be felt [N3-R5]. The evidence also notes that uterosacral ligament nodularity and firm nodules on rectovaginal or bimanual exam strongly suggest deep infiltrating endometriosis [N3-R2]. By contrast, nonspecific findings include tenderness in the pelvis, pain provoked by pressure, or findings that can be explained by other pelvic conditions rather than endometriosis [N3-R5]. The pelvic exam should therefore be interpreted alongside the history and other diagnostic clues rather than as a standalone test.

### When and how to perform rectovaginal or other specialized exams
Rectovaginal examination is indicated when the clinician needs better characterization of the posterior pelvis [N3-F3]. The evidence also supports this approach because it can help identify uterosacral nodules and other deep infiltrating findings [N3-R2]. However, in adolescents, this exam should be performed carefully and only when clinically indicated. The evidence notes that internal pelvic examination should be limited to sexually active patients, and may not be feasible due to anxiety, patient expectations, or pain [N1-F1]. Thus, rectovaginal or specialized exams should be reserved for cases where the history and initial exam raise suspicion of deep endometriosis, and performed with clear communication and patient consent [N3-F3].

### How to document findings in a way that supports diagnosis
Documentation should be thorough and structured. The evidence emphasizes that findings should be recorded in a way that supports diagnosis, including details of tenderness, nodule characteristics, and the location of pain [N3-R5]. It also notes that physical findings are part of the broader diagnostic workup, not just a routine exam [N3-F3]. A helpful approach is to record whether uterosacral ligaments are thickened or tender, whether posterior uterine tenderness is present, and whether rectovaginal examination reveals firm nodules or other suspicious findings [N3-R2][N3-R5]. These notes help distinguish endometriosis from nonspecific pelvic pain and support subsequent imaging or specialist referral [N3-F3].

Differentiating endometriosis from other causes of pelvic pain in adolescents requires combining history, physical findings, and red flags with a broad differential diagnosis. The evidence shows that adolescents with endometriosis often present with dysmenorrhea, chronic pelvic pain, and pain that worsens with bowel movement, urination, or sexual activity [N2-R2][N2-R5]. At the same time, many pelvic pain conditions in adolescents overlap with functional or musculoskeletal causes, making endometriosis harder to diagnose without careful evaluation [N2-F2].

### Red flags that point toward endometriosis rather than a different diagnosis
The strongest red flags for endometriosis in adolescents include:
- Dysmenorrhea that is severe or worsening despite treatment [N1-F1][N2-R2]
- Pelvic pain that worsens with bowel movement, urination, or sexual activity [N2-R5]
- Tenderness or nodules on pelvic exam, especially along uterosacral ligaments or posterior uterus [N3-R2][N3-R5]
- A history of delayed diagnosis and normalization of dysmenorrhea [N1-F1]
- Family history of endometriosis or related conditions [N6-R3][N6-R4]

These red flags help distinguish endometriosis from other pelvic pain conditions by linking symptoms to anatomical or hormonal mechanisms rather than purely functional or musculoskeletal causes [N2-F2]. The evidence also emphasizes that adolescents with endometriosis may present with nonmenstrual pelvic pain, which should not be dismissed as “just growing pains” [N2-F2].

### Non-endometriosis causes that must be considered
The differential diagnosis is broad. The evidence includes several important non-endometriosis causes:
- Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)
- Ovarian torsion
- Ruptured ovarian cyst
- Appendicitis
- Ovarian cysts and other gynecological/obstetrical causes [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]
- Functional pain conditions, including irritable bowel syndrome, vulvodynia, fibromyalgia, chronic migraine, and interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome [N2-F2]
- Myofascial pain and other musculoskeletal causes [N2-F2]

These conditions must be considered because they can mimic endometriosis, especially when adolescents present with chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, or pain related to activity or intercourse [N2-F2][N2-R4]. The evidence also highlights that CPP can have multiple contributing conditions, including gynecologic pathology and functional pain syndromes [N2-F2].

### When imaging is indicated and what it can show
Imaging is indicated when the history and physical exam are inconclusive, or when endometriosis is suspected despite a negative physical exam. The evidence supports ultrasound and MRI as the main imaging modalities [N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-R5]. A transabdominal ultrasound is helpful for identifying ovarian endometriomas but has a limited role in evaluating deep endometriosis [N4-R1]. MRI is particularly useful for rectosigmoid endometriosis and for treatment planning [N4-R4]. The UpToDate guidance also notes that MRI and transvaginal ultrasonography are recommended in the evaluation of suspected endometriosis [N6-R5]. In adolescents, MRI is often preferred when transvaginal ultrasound is not feasible or informative [N4-R5].

### When referral to a specialist is appropriate
Referral to a specialist should be considered when the diagnosis remains uncertain, when symptoms are refractory to first-line treatment, or when imaging suggests deep or complex endometriosis. The evidence supports specialist involvement because adolescents may need a multidisciplinary approach, especially if there is ongoing pain despite medical treatment [N1-F1][N6-R3]. Laparoscopic findings may also guide management [N4-R5]. The evidence further notes that adolescents with endometriosis may require counseling on menstrual suppression and may benefit from a multi-disciplinary team for chronic pain management [N1-F1]. Therefore, referral to a gynecologist or endometriosis specialist is appropriate when history, physical findings, and imaging do not confirm a clear alternative diagnosis, or when the adolescent’s pain is not adequately controlled with initial treatment [N4-R2][N6-R3].

The initial patient history for adolescents suspected of endometriosis should be comprehensive but developmentally sensitive. The evidence supports a history that includes menstrual history, dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain characteristics, sexual and reproductive history, family history, and psychosocial context [N1-F1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. This approach is especially important in adolescents, because pain normalization and delayed diagnosis are common [N1-F1].

### Symptoms and symptom patterns that are most informative
The most informative symptoms are dysmenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, and acyclic pelvic pain [N1-R5]. The evidence also notes that nonmenstrual pelvic pain can occur, and that pain may be aggravated by activity, intercourse, bowel movements, or urination [N2-R2][N2-R5]. Pain patterns that are particularly concerning for endometriosis include severe dysmenorrhea that does not improve with standard treatment, pain that worsens with bowel movement or urination, and pain that is provoked during gynecologic examination [N1-F1][N2-R5]. The evidence also emphasizes that adolescents may report other associated symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headaches, tiredness, back pain, and irritable mood [N2-R3].

### Menstrual history, including age of menarche and cycle regularity
Menstrual history is central to the evaluation. The evidence notes that age of menarche, cycle regularity, duration of menses, and the time elapsed between onset of menarche and dysmenorrhea should be elicited [N1-F1]. This is important because primary dysmenorrhea is often associated with anovulatory cycles and usually presents 6–12 months post-menarche [N1-F1]. Secondary dysmenorrhea, by contrast, is associated with pelvic pathology and may be more severe or persistent [N1-F1]. The evidence also highlights that adolescents should be asked about the degree of functional impairment, including absence or avoidance of school, social, and sports activities [N1-F1].

### Pelvic pain characteristics and how they relate to activity or intercourse
Pelvic pain should be described in terms of onset, duration, severity, aggravating and alleviating factors, and relationship to menses [N1-F1]. The evidence specifically notes that pain may be cyclic, acyclic, or accompanied by bowel or urinary symptoms [N1-F1]. It also states that endometriosis pain can worsen with bowel movement or urination and can be associated with painful tampon insertion or dyspareunia [N2-R5]. These details are important because they help distinguish endometriosis from other pelvic pain conditions, especially functional pain syndromes [N2-F2].

### Sexual and reproductive history relevant to diagnosis
Sexual and reproductive history is relevant because endometriosis may present with dyspareunia, and adolescents may also have a history of sexually transmitted infections or sexual violence [N1-F1]. The evidence notes that the first assessment should include a sexual history, including presence of dyspareunia, history of sexually transmitted or pelvic infections, and sexual violence [N1-F1]. It also notes that previous treatment, including medications, dosage, and timing, should be documented [N1-F1]. This history is important for assessing the full burden of pain and identifying conditions that may overlap with endometriosis [N2-F2].

### Family history of endometriosis or related conditions
Family history is an important red flag. The evidence notes that endometriosis should be considered in adolescents who experience ongoing pain despite medical treatment [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that the first assessment should include a family history of endometriosis or related conditions [N6-R3]. Family history is especially useful because endometriosis is genetically influenced and may run in families [N6-R3]. Including family history helps identify patients at higher risk and supports early investigation [N6-R3].

### Psychosocial and developmental context that may affect symptom reporting
The psychosocial and developmental context is central to history-taking in adolescents. The evidence states that adolescents should be interviewed with caregivers and independently, because parental modeling may influence pain reporting and perception [N1-F1]. It also notes that health care practitioners should not normalize dysmenorrhea, because normalization can delay diagnosis and treatment [N1-F1]. Adolescents may also experience anxiety, depression, and impaired quality of life, which can affect symptom reporting and functional impairment [N1-F1][N7-R4]. The evidence further notes that the impact of dysmenorrhea on quality of life is exacerbated by severity of pain and delay of diagnosis [N7-R5]. Therefore, the history should include questions about school attendance, social and sports activities, and emotional well-being [N1-F1].

Adolescents with endometriosis present differently from adults, and this has important diagnostic implications. The evidence shows that adolescents often experience dysmenorrhea and pelvic pain that is normalized or delayed in diagnosis because it is common for them to endure pain without seeking timely evaluation [N1-F1]. Adolescents can also present with symptoms that overlap with functional pain syndromes, making endometriosis harder to distinguish from other pelvic pain conditions [N2-F2].

### How adolescents with endometriosis differ from adult patients
Adolescents differ from adults in several ways. First, they often present with dysmenorrhea that is severe or persistent despite treatment, and this can be the first sign of endometriosis [N1-F1][N2-R2]. Second, adolescents may experience pain that worsens with bowel movement, urination, or sexual activity, which can be a red flag for deep endometriosis [N2-R5]. Third, adolescents may have a family history of endometriosis or related conditions, which increases suspicion [N6-R3]. Fourth, adolescents may be more likely to normalize pain, which delays diagnosis and treatment [N1-F1]. Finally, adolescents may require a more developmentally sensitive approach because they may not fully articulate their symptoms, and parental modeling can influence pain reporting [N1-F1]. Overall, adolescents with endometriosis often present with overlapping symptoms, delayed recognition, and a need for careful history-taking [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### Common diagnostic delays and normalization of dysmenorrhea
Normalization of dysmenorrhea is a major diagnostic delay. The evidence explicitly states that most adolescents will experience discomfort during menstruation and that normalization of dysmenorrhea leads to delay in diagnosis and treatment [N1-F1]. It also notes that adolescents may present later for assessment, see multiple physicians, and suffer more compared to adults [N1-F1]. The evidence further says that functional impairment is the primary reason for seeking medical care in adolescents with dysmenorrhea [N1-F1]. These findings show that adolescents often do not seek help early, and that clinicians must avoid normalizing pain in order to identify endometriosis sooner [N1-F1].

### Guidelines and recommendations for evaluation in adolescents
Guidelines recommend a structured, patient-centered approach. The evidence supports asking about age of menarche, cycle regularity, duration of menses, time elapsed between menarche and dysmenorrhea, onset, duration, severity, aggravating and alleviating factors, and relationship to menses [N1-F1]. It also recommends documenting urinary, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, and psychological symptoms, as well as functional impairment [N1-F1]. The UpToDate evidence states that the first assessment should include medical, gynecologic, menstrual, family, and psychosocial history [N6-R3][N6-R4]. AAFP guidance also emphasizes that physical examination should include a pelvic examination checking for tenderness or nodules of the cul-de-sac or uterosacral ligaments [N6-R2]. The evidence also supports specialist referral when symptoms persist despite first-line treatment or when imaging suggests deep endometriosis [N4-R2][N6-R3].

### Limitations of history alone versus need for imaging
History alone has limitations because adolescents may normalize pain, may underreport symptoms, or may present with symptoms that overlap with functional pain conditions [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that adolescents may require imaging when first-line treatments do not improve symptoms [N1-F1]. Imaging is indicated when the history and physical exam are inconclusive, or when endometriosis is suspected despite a negative physical exam [N4-R2]. The evidence supports ultrasound and MRI as the main imaging modalities, with transabdominal ultrasound helpful for ovarian endometriomas and MRI preferred for rectosigmoid endometriosis and treatment planning [N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R5]. Therefore, history should be followed by a focused physical exam and, when appropriate, imaging, because endometriosis cannot be reliably diagnosed from history alone [N4-R2][N6-R5].

Physical examination for adolescents suspected of endometriosis should be focused, patient-centered, and guided by the clinical context rather than a routine full genital exam. The evidence supports a careful pelvic exam that includes external genitalia, a speculum and bimanual exam, and, under some circumstances, a rectovaginal exam [N3-F3]. For adolescents, this is particularly important because the exam should be performed in a way that respects developmental and psychosocial context, and because internal pelvic examination may be limited or delayed if the adolescent is anxious, has pain, or is not sexually active [N1-F1].

### Components of a focused pelvic exam appropriate for adolescents
A focused adolescent pelvic exam should begin with inspection of the external genitalia and then proceed to a speculum and bimanual exam [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that rectovaginal examination may be appropriate when better characterization of the posterior pelvis is needed [N3-F3]. In adolescents, the exam should be adapted to the patient’s readiness, anxiety level, and ability to tolerate internal examination. The same source emphasizes that external genitalia and internal genitalia are both part of the pelvic exam [N3-F3]. The UpToDate evidence similarly states that physical examination should include a pelvic examination that checks for tenderness or nodules of the cul-de-sac or uterosacral ligaments [N6-R2]. That is a helpful shorthand for what should be palpated during a focused exam.

### Findings that are suggestive of endometriosis versus nonspecific findings
The most suggestive endometriosis findings on exam are tender nodules along thickened uterosacral ligaments, posterior uterus, or other sites where deep infiltrating endometriosis can be felt [N3-R5]. The evidence also notes that uterosacral ligament nodularity and firm nodules on rectovaginal or bimanual exam strongly suggest deep infiltrating endometriosis [N3-R2]. By contrast, nonspecific findings include tenderness in the pelvis, pain provoked by pressure, or findings that can be explained by other pelvic conditions rather than endometriosis [N3-R5]. The pelvic exam should therefore be interpreted alongside the history and other diagnostic clues rather than as a standalone test.

### When and how to perform rectovaginal or other specialized exams
Rectovaginal examination is indicated when the clinician needs better characterization of the posterior pelvis [N3-F3]. The evidence also supports this approach because it can help identify uterosacral nodules and other deep infiltrating findings [N3-R2]. However, in adolescents, this exam should be performed carefully and only when clinically indicated. The evidence notes that internal pelvic examination should be limited to sexually active patients, and may not be feasible due to anxiety, patient expectations, or pain [N1-F1]. Thus, rectovaginal or specialized exams should be reserved for cases where the history and initial exam raise suspicion of deep endometriosis, and performed with clear communication and patient consent [N3-F3].

### How to document findings in a way that supports diagnosis
Documentation should be thorough and structured. The evidence emphasizes that findings should be recorded in a way that supports diagnosis, including details of tenderness, nodule characteristics, and the location of pain [N3-R5]. It also notes that physical findings are part of the broader diagnostic workup, not just a routine exam [N3-F3]. A helpful approach is to record whether uterosacral ligaments are thickened or tender, whether posterior uterine tenderness is present, and whether rectovaginal examination reveals firm nodules or other suspicious findings [N3-R2][N3-R5]. These notes help distinguish endometriosis from nonspecific pelvic pain and support subsequent imaging or specialist referral [N3-F3].

Differentiating endometriosis from other causes of pelvic pain in adolescents requires combining history, physical findings, and red flags with a broad differential diagnosis. The evidence shows that adolescents with endometriosis often present with dysmenorrhea, chronic pelvic pain, and pain that worsens with bowel movement, urination, or sexual activity [N2-R2][N2-R5]. At the same time, many pelvic pain conditions in adolescents overlap with functional or musculoskeletal causes, making endometriosis harder to diagnose without careful evaluation [N2-F2].

### Red flags that point toward endometriosis rather than a different diagnosis
The strongest red flags for endometriosis in adolescents include:
- Dysmenorrhea that is severe or worsening despite treatment [N1-F1][N2-R2]
- Pelvic pain that worsens with bowel movement, urination, or sexual activity [N2-R5]
- Tenderness or nodules on pelvic exam, especially along uterosacral ligaments or posterior uterus [N3-R2][N3-R5]
- A history of delayed diagnosis and normalization of dysmenorrhea [N1-F1]
- Family history of endometriosis or related conditions [N6-R3][N6-R4]

These red flags help distinguish endometriosis from other pelvic pain conditions by linking symptoms to anatomical or hormonal mechanisms rather than purely functional or musculoskeletal causes [N2-F2]. The evidence also emphasizes that adolescents with endometriosis may present with nonmenstrual pelvic pain, which should not be dismissed as “just growing pains” [N2-F2].

### Non-endometriosis causes that must be considered
The differential diagnosis is broad. The evidence includes several important non-endometriosis causes:
- Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)
- Ovarian torsion
- Ruptured ovarian cyst
- Appendicitis
- Ovarian cysts and other gynecological/obstetrical causes [N5-R1][N5-R4][N5-R5]
- Functional pain conditions, including irritable bowel syndrome, vulvodynia, fibromyalgia, chronic migraine, and interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome [N2-F2]
- Myofascial pain and other musculoskeletal causes [N2-F2]

These conditions must be considered because they can mimic endometriosis, especially when adolescents present with chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, or pain related to activity or intercourse [N2-F2][N2-R4]. The evidence also highlights that CPP can have multiple contributing conditions, including gynecologic pathology and functional pain syndromes [N2-F2].

### When imaging is indicated and what it can show
Imaging is indicated when the history and physical exam are inconclusive, or when endometriosis is suspected despite a negative physical exam. The evidence supports ultrasound and MRI as the main imaging modalities [N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-R5]. A transabdominal ultrasound is helpful for identifying ovarian endometriomas but has a limited role in evaluating deep endometriosis [N4-R1]. MRI is particularly useful for rectosigmoid endometriosis and for treatment planning [N4-R4]. The UpToDate guidance also notes that MRI and transvaginal ultrasonography are recommended in the evaluation of suspected endometriosis [N6-R5]. In adolescents, MRI is often preferred when transvaginal ultrasound is not feasible or informative [N4-R5].

### When referral to a specialist is appropriate
Referral to a specialist should be considered when the diagnosis remains uncertain, when symptoms are refractory to first-line treatment, or when imaging suggests deep or complex endometriosis. The evidence supports specialist involvement because adolescents may need a multidisciplinary approach, especially if there is ongoing pain despite medical treatment [N1-F1][N6-R3]. Laparoscopic findings may also guide management [N4-R5]. The evidence further notes that adolescents with endometriosis may require counseling on menstrual suppression and may benefit from a multi-disciplinary team for chronic pain management [N1-F1]. Therefore, referral to a gynecologist or endometriosis specialist is appropriate when history, physical findings, and imaging do not confirm a clear alternative diagnosis, or when the adolescent’s pain is not adequately controlled with initial treatment [N4-R2][N6-R3].

The initial patient history for adolescents suspected of endometriosis should be comprehensive but developmentally sensitive. The evidence supports a history that includes menstrual history, dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain characteristics, sexual and reproductive history, family history, and psychosocial context [N1-F1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. This approach is especially important in adolescents, because pain normalization and delayed diagnosis are common [N1-F1].

### Symptoms and symptom patterns that are most informative
The most informative symptoms are dysmenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, and acyclic pelvic pain [N1-R5]. The evidence also notes that nonmenstrual pelvic pain can occur, and that pain may be aggravated by activity, intercourse, bowel movements, or urination [N2-R2][N2-R5]. Pain patterns that are particularly concerning for endometriosis include severe dysmenorrhea that does not improve with standard treatment, pain that worsens with bowel movement or urination, and pain that is provoked during gynecologic examination [N1-F1][N2-R5]. The evidence also emphasizes that adolescents may report other associated symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headaches, tiredness, back pain, and irritable mood [N2-R3].

### Menstrual history, including age of menarche and cycle regularity
Menstrual history is central to the evaluation. The evidence notes that age of menarche, cycle regularity, duration of menses, and the time elapsed between onset of menarche and dysmenorrhea should be elicited [N1-F1]. This is important because primary dysmenorrhea is often associated with anovulatory cycles and usually presents 6–12 months post-menarche [N1-F1]. Secondary dysmenorrhea, by contrast, is associated with pelvic pathology and may be more severe or persistent [N1-F1]. The evidence also highlights that adolescents should be asked about the degree of functional impairment, including absence or avoidance of school, social, and sports activities [N1-F1].

### Pelvic pain characteristics and how they relate to activity or intercourse
Pelvic pain should be described in terms of onset, duration, severity, aggravating and alleviating factors, and relationship to menses [N1-F1]. The evidence specifically notes that pain may be cyclic, acyclic, or accompanied by bowel or urinary symptoms [N1-F1]. It also states that endometriosis pain can worsen with bowel movement or urination and can be associated with painful tampon insertion or dyspareunia [N2-R5]. These details are important because they help distinguish endometriosis from other pelvic pain conditions, especially functional pain syndromes [N2-F2].

### Sexual and reproductive history relevant to diagnosis
Sexual and reproductive history is relevant because endometriosis may present with dyspareunia, and adolescents may also have a history of sexually transmitted infections or sexual violence [N1-F1]. The evidence notes that the first assessment should include a sexual history, including presence of dyspareunia, history of sexually transmitted or pelvic infections, and sexual violence [N1-F1]. It also notes that previous treatment, including medications, dosage, and timing, should be documented [N1-F1]. This history is important for assessing the full burden of pain and identifying conditions that may overlap with endometriosis [N2-F2].

### Family history of endometriosis or related conditions
Family history is an important red flag. The evidence notes that endometriosis should be considered in adolescents who experience ongoing pain despite medical treatment [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that the first assessment should include a family history of endometriosis or related conditions [N6-R3]. Family history is especially useful because endometriosis is genetically influenced and may run in families [N6-R3]. Including family history helps identify patients at higher risk and supports early investigation [N6-R3].

### Psychosocial and developmental context that may affect symptom reporting
The psychosocial and developmental context is central to history-taking in adolescents. The evidence states that adolescents should be interviewed with caregivers and independently, because parental modeling may influence pain reporting and perception [N1-F1]. It also notes that health care practitioners should not normalize dysmenorrhea, because normalization can delay diagnosis and treatment [N1-F1]. Adolescents may also experience anxiety, depression, and impaired quality of life, which can affect symptom reporting and functional impairment [N1-F1][N7-R4]. The evidence further notes that the impact of dysmenorrhea on quality of life is exacerbated by severity of pain and delay of diagnosis [N7-R5]. Therefore, the history should include questions about school attendance, social and sports activities, and emotional well-being [N1-F1].

Adolescents with endometriosis present differently from adults, and this has important diagnostic implications. The evidence shows that adolescents often experience dysmenorrhea and pelvic pain that is normalized or delayed in diagnosis because it is common for them to endure pain without seeking timely evaluation [N1-F1]. Adolescents can also present with symptoms that overlap with functional pain syndromes, making endometriosis harder to distinguish from other pelvic pain conditions [N2-F2].

### How adolescents with endometriosis differ from adult patients
Adolescents differ from adults in several ways. First, they often present with dysmenorrhea that is severe or persistent despite treatment, and this can be the first sign of endometriosis [N1-F1][N2-R2]. Second, adolescents may experience pain that worsens with bowel movement, urination, or sexual activity, which can be a red flag for deep endometriosis [N2-R5]. Third, adolescents may have a family history of endometriosis or related conditions, which increases suspicion [N6-R3]. Fourth, adolescents may be more likely to normalize pain, which delays diagnosis and treatment [N1-F1]. Finally, adolescents may require a more developmentally sensitive approach because they may not fully articulate their symptoms, and parental modeling can influence pain reporting [N1-F1]. Overall, adolescents with endometriosis often present with overlapping symptoms, delayed recognition, and a need for careful history-taking [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### Common diagnostic delays and normalization of dysmenorrhea
Normalization of dysmenorrhea is a major diagnostic delay. The evidence explicitly states that most adolescents will experience discomfort during menstruation and that normalization of dysmenorrhea leads to delay in diagnosis and treatment [N1-F1]. It also notes that adolescents may present later for assessment, see multiple physicians, and suffer more compared to adults [N1-F1]. The evidence further says that functional impairment is the primary reason for seeking medical care in adolescents with dysmenorrhea [N1-F1]. These findings show that adolescents often do not seek help early, and that clinicians must avoid normalizing pain in order to identify endometriosis sooner [N1-F1].

### Guidelines and recommendations for evaluation in adolescents
Guidelines recommend a structured, patient-centered approach. The evidence supports asking about age of menarche, cycle regularity, duration of menses, time elapsed between menarche and dysmenorrhea, onset, duration, severity, aggravating and alleviating factors, and relationship to menses [N1-F1]. It also recommends documenting urinary, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, and psychological symptoms, as well as functional impairment [N1-F1]. The UpToDate evidence states that the first assessment should include medical, gynecologic, menstrual, family, and psychosocial history [N6-R3][N6-R4]. AAFP guidance also emphasizes that physical examination should include a pelvic examination checking for tenderness or nodules of the cul-de-sac or uterosacral ligaments [N6-R2]. The evidence also supports specialist referral when symptoms persist despite first-line treatment or when imaging suggests deep endometriosis [N4-R2][N6-R3].

### Limitations of history alone versus need for imaging
History alone has limitations because adolescents may normalize pain, may underreport symptoms, or may present with symptoms that overlap with functional pain conditions [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that adolescents may require imaging when first-line treatments do not improve symptoms [N1-F1]. The evidence notes that internal pelvic examination should be limited to sexually active patients, and may not be feasible due to anxiety, patient expectations, or pain [N1-F1]. Documentation should be thorough and structured. Adolescents with endometriosis present differently from adults, and this has important diagnostic implications. Normalization of dysmenorrhea is a major diagnostic delay. 1. A thorough, developmentally sensitive history covering dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, menstrual history, sexual and reproductive history, family history, and psychosocial context [N1-F1][N6-R3][N6-R4][N7-R4].
